title: Writing text and formatted data to files
learningObjectives: Explain the C concept and its rules.
Trace the example and describe data flow.
Identify relevant failure and boundary cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: A FILE stream can receive character, string and formatted output through functions such as fputc, fputs and fprintf. These functions report failures through their return values; buffered output may not reach the underlying file until a flush or close.
understand.whyItMatters: Checking write results prevents a program from reporting success when storage is full, a device fails or the stream becomes invalid.
understand.analogy: Treat the operation as a clearly specified contract between the program and its data.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's type, lifetime, I/O and object representation rules.

explain.narrative:
A FILE stream can receive character, string and formatted output through functions such as fputc, fputs and fprintf. These functions report failures through their return values; buffered output may not reach the underlying file until a flush or close.

Check all return values, object lifetimes, types and preconditions. Enable compiler warnings and test expected as well as failure paths.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: fprintf writes formatted text and returns a nonnegative count on success. fclose is checked because pending buffered output can fail during close.

practise.guidedTask: Identify both possible failure points in the example.
practise.independentTask: Write a report containing several records. Check each output operation and the final close.
hints: Use format specifiers that match the supplied argument types.
Do not treat a successful fprintf as proof that data is safely stored on durable media.
Check the return values of writes and fclose.
